clue.text: Rogue I phone back to get car

indicators.note: to send something back is to return it the way it came, so the word is written right to left

blocks.note: a cad is a dishonourable man, a rogue
taken as written
to phone someone is to call them

explanation.surface: A crook who has stolen a car rings up to get it back to its owner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Phone back' reads like returning a call, but it asks for the word for phone written backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cadillac is a famous American luxury automobile brand made by General Motors.

clue.text: Principles require writing off half of core debt

indicators.note: writing something off cancels it, so half of each word is cancelled and dropped

blocks.note: the front half of the four-letter word
the front half of the four-letter word

explanation.surface: A bank's guiding rules demand that half of its central debt be cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Core debt' looks like a financial phrase, but the halving applies to each word separately, keeping the first two letters of both.
explanation.definitionFit: A code is a set of rules or moral standards, as in a code of conduct or ethics.

clue.text: Colours for duke getting approval

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for duke
saying yes gives approval

explanation.surface: A duke's regimental colours are approved by royal decree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colours' suggests heraldic flags in the surface, but here it means substances used to tint fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyes are pigments or tints used to stain cloth, so colours in the plural noun sense.

clue.text: In the middle of slow etudes, Berg provided added volume

definitions.note: the answer is a comparative adjective, 'with added volume'

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, so only the centre of each word is kept

blocks.note: the two central letters of a four-letter word
the two central letters of a six-letter word
the two central letters of the composer's name

explanation.surface: Partway through some slow studies, the composer Alban Berg boosted the volume.
explanation.walkthrough: The middles of three consecutive words are taken: LO, UD and ER make LOUDER. An etude is a short musical study, which suits the composer in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Something louder has more volume or sound, a straightforward comparative of loud.

clue.text: Perfect request for dessert

definitions.note: adjective for the noun phrase; things 'in apple-pie order' are perfect

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for flawless neatness
second meaning: literally asking a waiter for a fruit pudding

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'in apple-pie order' means perfectly neat; read literally, the same words are a diner ordering a pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes everything arranged neatly and tidily, while a diner's order for a fruit pie fits the literal reading.

clue.text: Open aid distributed through peace group

indicators.note: spreading letters throughout something scatters them into new positions

blocks.note: taken as written
the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, a British peace movement

explanation.surface: A charity's aid is handed out openly through a peace organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: CND is the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, Britain's best-known peace group; the letters of aid are spread among its letters to give C-A-N-D-I-D.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone candid is frank and honest, speaking their mind openly without concealment.

clue.text: Top-ranking wager covers everything used here

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase rather than a noun

blocks.note: alpha means first or dominant, as in alpha male
a bet is a wager

explanation.surface: A high-stakes gamble includes everything on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here' means the crossword itself: every letter in the grid comes from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Every word in the puzzle is spelt from the twenty-six letters of the English writing system.

clue.text: Passed over hard liquor when depressed

indicators.note: lying over something covers it on both sides, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: 'passed' is a euphemism for died
spirits are strong distilled drinks

explanation.surface: Someone who felt low turned down the strong drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed over' reads as declined, but 'passed' alone is the euphemism for died and 'over' tells it to go around the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dispirited means having lost heart, feeling low and gloomy, which is a synonym.

clue.text: Wild sandy shores lose initial hydration when it doesn't rain

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for the times named by the plural noun

indicators.note: something wild is unruly and out of order, so the letters are rearranged
to lose something is to be without it, so a letter is dropped
initial means at the start, so only the first letter is meant

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Untamed sandy beaches dry out when there is no rainfall.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the H from SANDY SHORES, then rearrange the remaining ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry seasons are periods of the year in tropical climates with little or no rainfall.

clue.text: Run-down property due proper reconstruction

indicators.note: a reconstruction rebuilds something in a new form, so the letters are rebuilt in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dilapidated house is due a thorough rebuild.
explanation.walkthrough: A doer-upper is British estate-agent slang for a house that needs renovating.
explanation.definitionFit: A doer-upper is a dilapidated house sold cheaply because the buyer must renovate it.

clue.text: Shopping around for a cure?

blocks.note: surface reading: comparing pharmacies for the best medicine
setter's reading: going shopping to cheer yourself up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shopping around' suggests hunting for the best price on medicine; the cure is the mood lift that buying things brings.
explanation.definitionFit: The jokey phrase describes buying things to lift one's spirits, as if a spree were medical treatment.

clue.text: Aggressive, but the opposite when backup goes missing

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the little word is turned round

blocks.note: the word contains a little word that the front half sends the other way
the opposite of aggressive is timid

explanation.surface: Someone is forceful, yet becomes the reverse once their support disappears.
explanation.walkthrough: Take PU, which is 'up' backwards, off PUSHY and you are left with SHY, its opposite: so PU plus SHY builds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pushy person is forceful and overly assertive in getting what they want.

clue.text: Move some services out of Barking and Leicester?—

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, and mad letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Government offices are relocated from Barking, in east London, and the Midlands city of Leicester.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking looks like a place name beside Leicester, but it is the anagram signal: barking mad means crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: To decentralise is to transfer functions away from a central headquarters to regional offices.

clue.text: Sensitive types some say but they are all unique

blocks.note: first meaning: a disparaging slang term for easily offended people
second meaning: ice crystals famously never identical

explanation.walkthrough: 'Some say' flags that the first sense is an insult used by some people. The second is the old saying that no two ice crystals are alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang insult mocks people as fragile, and falling ice crystals are each said to have a different shape.

clue.text: Opera is a vital art with a twist

indicators.note: a twist bends something out of shape, so the letters are wrenched into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Opera is an essential art form, with a modern twist.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'a' after 'with' is part of the fodder too; without it there are only three of the four As.
explanation.definitionFit: La Traviata is Verdi's famous tragic opera about the courtesan Violetta.

clue.text: Newly elected American Republican starts being mean

indicators.note: the start of each word is its first letter, so only those are kept

blocks.note: first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A freshly elected US Republican starts off being stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like a verb but is the adjective for stingy; NEAR in this sense is old-fashioned British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Near is a dated British word for stingy or tight-fisted with money.

clue.text: TV drama production showing discomforts around home?

indicators.note: being around something surrounds it, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: miseries are sufferings or discomforts
being in is being at home

explanation.surface: A television drama depicts household troubles around the family home.
explanation.walkthrough: IN = at home is a common convention; it goes in after the first letter of MISERIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A mini-series is a television drama shown in a short run of episodes.

clue.text: Troubled after Charlie gets attacked

blocks.note: a Charlie is British slang for a fool
something that ailed you troubled you

explanation.surface: Someone upset after a person called Charlie is assaulted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' tells you the troubled part comes second. Calling someone 'a right Charlie' in Britain means they are a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail someone is to set upon them violently, so assailed is a synonym in the past tense.

clue.text: Poet who gives value for the text

blocks.note: a text is made of words
worth is value

explanation.surface: A poet makes every line of text count.
explanation.walkthrough: The value for the text is the words' worth, which is how the Romantic poet's name splits.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the English Romantic writer of the Lake District verse.

clue.text: Chopped up hake when gutted

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, leaving only the outer letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of the fish
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A fish is chopped into pieces once it has been cleaned out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When' looks like a link word, but it is gutted too, giving its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Hewn is the past participle of hew, meaning cut or hacked with an axe or blade.

clue.text: Promoted piece of exquisitely graceful diamond-based design

indicators.note: a piece is a part, so the letters are a run inside the words
promoted means moved up, and in a down clue that sends the letters upward

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A refined, elegant diamond-patterned design is being advertised.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'promoted' means read upwards, so the hidden run is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Argyle is the knitwear pattern of interlocking diamonds seen on socks and sweaters.

clue.text: Gain wisdom breaking naval red line

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it apart, so the letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Learning by experience after crossing a navy's red line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' reads as crossing the line, but it signals rearranging all twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying means becoming wiser through experience, especially after making mistakes.

clue.text: Highest recommendation by a California wine area

blocks.note: in British horse racing a tipster's nap is their most confident tip of the day
taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic's top recommendation for a Californian wine region.
explanation.walkthrough: A nap is a racing tipster's surest bet of the day, a term from British newspaper racing pages.
explanation.definitionFit: The Napa Valley north of San Francisco is America's best-known wine-growing region.

clue.text: Charge recruiting tenor for fundraiser

indicators.note: recruiting takes someone into an organisation, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: a fee is a charge
T is the abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: An entry charge is levied to hire a tenor singer for a charity event.
explanation.walkthrough: A fete is a British outdoor fair, often run to raise money for a church or school.
explanation.definitionFit: A village fete is an outdoor event with stalls and games held to raise funds.

clue.text: Songbird going back over a village in Africa

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word reads right to left
lying over something covers it, so one piece is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: the lark is a songbird
taken as written

explanation.surface: A songbird flies back over an African village.
explanation.walkthrough: Reverse LARK to KRAL, then put A inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A kraal is a traditional southern African settlement of huts, or an enclosure for livestock.

clue.text: Money earned available immediately

blocks.note: the ready, or readies, is British slang for cash
money you earned is money you made

explanation.surface: Wages that can be drawn straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The readies' is British slang for cash in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready-made goods are prepared in advance, so they can be bought and used at once.

clue.text: Quiet and young? This drink's allowed perhaps

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the drink

blocks.note: sh is the call for silence
taken as written
Y is the abbreviation for young

explanation.surface: Is a quiet youngster permitted this drink?
explanation.walkthrough: A shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, weak enough that a young person might be allowed it: so the wordplay doubles as the reason.
explanation.definitionFit: Shandy is a low-alcohol British mix of beer and lemonade, often given to teenagers.

clue.text: Class profile every word here displays

definitions.note: a descriptive clause rather than a noun

blocks.note: a type is a class or kind
a profile is a side view of the face

explanation.surface: A class profile shows off every word written in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here' is the printed crossword: every clue word appears in some font.
explanation.definitionFit: A typeface is the printed style of lettering, a font in which all printed text appears.
